title: Sudden painful finger overnight in a 36-year-old fisherman
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 36-year-old fisherman in the ED. He woke overnight with a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender left ring finger DIP joint, and had a self-limiting big toe attack last year. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, bloods, joint aspirate and hand X-ray. They then diagnose acute gout while keeping septic arthritis in view, manage the flare, and counsel him on preventing further attacks, red flags and follow-up.
focus: Acute monoarthritis: diagnosing recurrent gout, excluding septic arthritis, treating the flare and planning prevention
stem: You are a medical student on your emergency medicine rotation in the Emergency Department of a large metropolitan hospital. Mr Tan, a 36-year-old fisherman, has come in with severe joint pain. The ED registrar has asked you to assess him first. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Tan and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, blood results, joint aspirate results and hand X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Mr Tan, a 36-year-old fisherman. You are sitting on the trolley holding your left hand up against your chest and wincing whenever anyone comes near it. You are friendly but in a lot of pain and keen to get back to work. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "So last night I was suddenly woken up by my finger feeling like it was being burnt off..."

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: the end of your left ring finger. If asked to show exactly where, point to the last knuckle (the DIP joint). No other joints hurt.
  • Handedness (only if asked): you are left-handed.
  • Character: a severe burning ache.
  • Severity: 8 to 9 out of 10. It woke you from sleep.
  • Onset and course: it came on suddenly last night. It has been constant since and is getting worse.
  • Aggravating and relieving factors: worse if you move the finger or anything presses on it. Even the bedsheet hurt. Nothing has helped.
  • Previous episode: last year your big toe (at the base of the toe) went the same way: red, swollen and very painful. It settled by itself in about a week. You did not see a doctor.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No injury to the finger. No cuts, fish hook injuries, fin spikes, bites or skin breaks on the hands.
  • No fever, sweats or shakes. You do not feel generally unwell.
  • No recent illness: no sore throat, no diarrhoea, no burning when passing urine or discharge.
  • No pain or swelling in other joints. No stiffness in the mornings. No pain that comes on with use, and no locking or clicking of joints.
  • No skin rashes, scaly patches or nail changes. No lumps on the ears, elbows, fingers or toes.
  • No eye or bowel problems.

Past medical history

  • Nil. You do not see a doctor much. No kidney problems, high blood pressure or stomach ulcers that you know of.
  • You know you are overweight.

Medications and allergies

  • No regular medicines, no over-the-counter tablets and no supplements.
  • Allergy: peanuts. Only if asked what happens: "My throat swells up and I can't breathe. I had to go to hospital as a kid."

Family history

  • Nil. No gout, arthritis or other joint or autoimmune problems in the family.

Social history

  • You are a fisherman and work with your hands all day: hauling nets and lines.
  • You live with your wife and your dog. You are well supported.
  • Smoking: 15 cigarettes a day since you were 15.
  • Alcohol: a glass of red wine every night with dinner. "I do love my red."
  • Diet: lots of fresh seafood. You bring home prawns, mussels and fish from the boat.
  • No regular exercise. Fully independent.
  • You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
  • Background (only if asked): your parents came from Malaysia; your family is Chinese.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "No idea, mate. I didn't do anything to it."
  • Concerns: you are worried about work because you cannot move the finger and it is your dominant hand. You are worried it is the same thing as last year: "Is it going to keep coming back?"
  • Expectations: you want relief from the pain, and you want to stop it happening again.

During the station

  • If the candidate offers ice, elevation or a pain killer early, thank them. If analgesia with a dose and ice are ordered, by the end of Part 1 say: "That's a bit better, maybe a 7 now." If nothing is offered, keep wincing and say about halfway: "Sorry, can I get something for the pain?"

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If the candidate orders analgesia, ice, a splint, bloods, an X-ray or a joint aspirate, says "I'll get that organised." If a drug is ordered without a dose or route, asks "What dose and route would you like?"
  • If the candidate asks for results, says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: alert, in obvious pain, guarding his left hand. Weight 112 kg, height 178 cm (BMI 35).
  • Observations: RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 146/90, HR 96 regular, temperature 37.4 °C, pain 8/10, CRT 2 seconds.
  • Left ring finger, look: the DIP joint is swollen, with red, shiny, tense skin over it. No skin break, puncture wound, splinter or foreign body. The rest of the finger is normal in size. Nails normal.
  • Feel: the DIP joint is hot and exquisitely tender; he pulls away from light touch. No tenderness along the flexor sheath on the palm side of the finger. No fluctuance.
  • Move: active and passive DIP movement are markedly reduced by pain. PIP and MCP joints move fully. The finger is not held flexed. Passive extension of the finger at the PIP and MCP joints does not cause pain along the palm side of the finger. Sensation and capillary refill in the fingertip are normal.
  • Spreading infection: no cellulitis on the hand, no red streaks up the forearm, no epitrochlear or axillary lymph nodes.
  • Other joints: the other finger joints, both wrists, elbows, knees, ankles and both first MTP joints are normal, with no swelling, warmth or tenderness.
  • Tophi: none on the ears, elbows, fingers or toes.
  • Skin and nails: no psoriatic plaques (elbows, knees, scalp, umbilicus), no nail pitting or onycholysis.

check.x: Professionalism
Introduces self and role, confirms the patient's identity, gains consent, explains confidentiality, and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Acknowledges his severe pain early, shows empathy about his work and his fear that it will keep coming back, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the joint pain:

kids.x: Site: tip of the left ring finger, at the DIP joint, with no other joint involved
Onset and course: sudden, woke him last night, constant and getting worse
Character and severity: severe burning ache, 8 to 9/10
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse on moving or pressing, nothing helps; establishes that he is left-handed (dominant hand)

check.x: Elicits a previous similar attack: the big toe last year, which settled by itself in about a week without seeing a doctor.
Explicitly considers septic arthritis and asks about:
check.d: Per the source marking, a candidate who never considers septic arthritis cannot score the differential marks in the history.

kids.x: Fever, sweats, rigors or feeling generally unwell
Skin breaks or penetrating injuries on the hand (fish hooks, fin spikes, cuts, bites)
Recent illness or infection (sore throat, diarrhoea, urethral discharge)

check.x: Asks about trauma to the finger (none).
Asks about at least two risk factors for gout: diet high in seafood or red meat, alcohol, weight, diuretics or low-dose aspirin, and kidney disease.

Screens for a polyarthropathy or another arthritis: other joints, prolonged morning stiffness (rheumatoid), pain on use or locking (osteoarthritis), psoriasis or nail changes (psoriatic), and lumps (tophi).
Takes the past history, medications and allergies:

kids.x: No past medical history, including no kidney disease, hypertension or peptic ulcer
No regular or over-the-counter medicines (no diuretics or aspirin)
Peanut allergy, and clarifies the reaction as anaphylaxis
kids.d: Mark only if the reaction is clarified.

check.x: Asks about family history of gout or rheumatological disease (none).

Takes a social history: fisherman, lives with his wife and dog and well supported, 15 cigarettes a day since 15 (about 16 pack-years), a glass of red wine every night, lots of fresh seafood, no regular exercise, independent.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea of the cause, worried about work, afraid it will keep coming back, wants pain relief and to stop it recurring.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations (afebrile at 37.4 °C, HR 96, BP 146/90) and weight or BMI (112 kg, BMI 35).
Inspects and palpates the left ring finger DIP joint and finds a red, shiny, swollen, hot and exquisitely tender joint, with no skin break, puncture wound or foreign body.

Assesses movement (active and passive DIP movement markedly reduced by pain) and checks for flexor sheath infection: swelling confined to the DIP, no tenderness along the sheath, finger not held flexed, and no pain on passive extension.
Looks for spreading infection: cellulitis, lymphangitis up the forearm, and epitrochlear or axillary nodes (none).
Examines the other joints, including both first MTP joints and the rest of the hand, and finds them normal.
Looks for tophi (ears, elbows, fingers, toes) and for psoriatic plaques and nail changes, and finds none.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all in the white zone (no vital-sign escalation criteria), afebrile but this does not exclude septic arthritis; pain still 7/10 after initial analgesia needs further analgesia (an NSAID now) and medical review.
Interprets the joint aspirate:

kids.x: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals confirm gout
WCC 18 000 ×10^6/L with 85% neutrophils is inflammatory, which fits crystal arthritis and is below the level typical of septic arthritis (usually above 50 000)
Gram stain is negative but culture is pending (preliminary at 48 hours, final at 5 days), and crystals do not exclude infection in the same joint

check.x: Interprets the bloods: raised CRP, ESR and neutrophils fit inflammation but do not separate gout from infection; a urate within the reference range does not exclude gout because it can fall during a flare, so it is repeated after the flare; normal renal function makes an NSAID reasonable.
Interprets the hand X-ray: soft tissue swelling only. No fracture, foreign body, erosions or chondrocalcinosis, which is expected early in gout.

Gives acute gout of the left ring finger DIP joint (his second attack) as the diagnosis. Supports it with the sudden overnight onset, exquisite tenderness, the previous big toe attack, the seafood, nightly red wine and BMI 35, and the urate crystals.
Names at least three differentials, including septic arthritis, each with a feature for or against it, from: septic arthritis, pseudogout (CPPD), psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis and trauma.
Management
Starts symptomatic care promptly: rest, ice, elevation and a protective splint, plus paracetamol.
check.d: Credit if ordered in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Chooses an NSAID with a dose (for example naproxen 500 mg orally 12-hourly, or indometacin 50 mg orally 8-hourly) until the attack settles, with a PPI if he has GI risk factors (previous ulcer or bleed, age over 65, anticoagulant, antiplatelet or corticosteroid use); he has none, so a PPI is optional for a short course. First checks for contraindications: kidney disease, peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, asthma made worse by NSAIDs, cardiovascular disease and anticoagulants.
check.d: Credit a candidate who either gives a PPI or justifies leaving it out for a short course in a 36-year-old with no ulcer history.

check.x: States the alternatives if an NSAID is unsuitable, or as an equal alternative per eTG:

kids.x: Low-dose colchicine (1 mg, then 0.5 mg an hour later; maximum 1.5 mg per course, and do not repeat within 3 days), most effective when started early; warns about diarrhoea
A short course of oral prednisolone (for example 30 mg orally daily for 3 to 5 days), or an intra-articular corticosteroid once infection is excluded

check.x: Closes the loop on septic arthritis: follows up the synovial fluid culture until the final report at 5 days and the blood cultures, and recalls him for orthopaedic or hand team review and IV antibiotics if a culture is positive or he becomes febrile or worse.

Plans disposition: discharge home once the pain is controlled, with a written plan, a medical certificate and GP review in 1 to 2 weeks; does not use allopurinol to treat the attack, and leaves starting urate-lowering therapy to the GP with flare cover.
Explains gout in plain words: urate crystals forming in the joint, linked to diet, alcohol and weight, and likely to recur without changes.
Gives lifestyle advice covering at least three of: weight loss, cutting down alcohol, fewer purine-rich foods (shellfish, red and organ meat), fewer sugary drinks, quitting smoking (Quitline/GP).
Safety netting

Tells him in plain words to come straight back to ED for fever or shakes, spreading redness or red streaks up the hand or arm, or pain getting worse despite treatment, and that ED will phone him if the joint culture grows anything.
check.d: Credit-worthy extras, not required for the mark: stopping the NSAID and seeking help for black stools, vomiting blood or severe stomach pain; stopping colchicine for diarrhoea; calling 000 if very unwell.

check.x: Explains that a daily preventer tablet (allopurinol) is likely to be recommended after a second attack and will be arranged by the GP once the flare settles; it is taken long term to keep urate low, and he should stop it and seek help if a rash develops.
check.d: Credit-worthy extras, not required for the mark: repeating the urate 2 to 4 weeks after the flare; starting low and increasing to a urate below 0.36 mmol/L; cover against flares when starting. Febuxostat, probenecid, the specific prophylaxis options and HLA-B*5801 testing are teaching points only and are not required; a candidate who raises HLA-B*5801 because of his Chinese background may be noted favourably.

part2.lead: It is now 10:30. Here are Mr Tan's observations, his blood results, the result of the joint aspirate the orthopaedic registrar performed, and the report of his hand X-ray.
part2.patient:
Ask these only during the fourth question, once each, as the candidate explains.

Mr Tan is relieved to have an answer but keen to get back to work. As the candidate explains, ask these once each:

  • "So what is it? Is it the same as my toe last year?"
  • "Is it going to keep coming back?"
  • "Do I have to give up my red wine and prawns?"

If the candidate uses jargon ("urate", "crystals", "prophylaxis"), ask "What does that mean?" once. If told he can go home, ask: "When can I get back on the boat?" (Expected answer: back on the boat when the pain settles and he can grip, usually within a week; medical certificate given.)

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Weight 112 kg, height 178 cm. Joint aspirated at 09:30. 10:15 set: after initial analgesia and ice; post-aspiration.
handover.model:
• Read: at 07:40, 08:05 and 10:15: RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, systolic BP 140 to 146, HR 90 to 96 regular, temperature 37.4 to 37.5 °C, alert, CRT 2 seconds. All are in the white zone at all three times. Pain 8/10 at triage, 7/10 after initial analgesia; still poorly controlled.
  • Meaning: no systemic compromise. The mild tachycardia and BP fit severe pain, and he is afebrile. Absence of fever does not exclude septic arthritis.
  • Changes: no vital sign is in a yellow or red zone. Pain still poorly controlled: needs further analgesia (an NSAID now if not already given) and medical review. Repeat the observations, including temperature, before discharge.

rows.note: Triage ATS 3: hot swollen left ring finger, woke with pain overnight
Repeat set while awaiting medical review
After initial analgesia and ice; post-aspiration

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 08:20. Blood cultures × 2 collected at the same time: no growth to date (final report at 5 days).
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 11.8 with neutrophils 8.6 (mildly raised). CRP 38 and ESR 30 raised. Urate 0.40 mmol/L, within the reference range. Sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine normal, eGFR above 90. ALT 52 and GGT 68 mildly raised, with normal ALP, bilirubin and albumin. Random glucose 6.1.
  • Meaning: a systemic inflammatory response that fits an acute gout flare, though it does not separate gout from infection. Serum urate often falls during a flare, so a normal value does not exclude gout. Teaching point (not marked): 0.40 is above the 0.36 mmol/L target and at the saturation point of urate, so it supports a high urate load. The liver enzymes fit alcohol or fatty liver with BMI 35 (teaching point, not marked).
  • Changes: normal renal function means an NSAID is reasonable and allopurinol can later be started at the usual low dose (teaching point, not marked). Repeat the urate 2 to 4 weeks after the flare. Follow up the blood cultures.

rows.n: may fall during an acute attack

handover.label: Synovial fluid, left ring finger DIP joint
handover.result: Aspirated at 09:30 by the orthopaedic registrar under ultrasound guidance: 0.4 mL of cloudy yellow fluid. Culture: preliminary report at 48 hours, final at 5 days.
handover.model:
• Read: cloudy fluid with WCC 18 000 ×10^6/L and 85% neutrophils. Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals, inside and outside cells. Gram stain shows no organisms. Culture is pending.
  • Meaning: monosodium urate crystals confirm gout. The cell count is inflammatory and fits crystal arthritis; septic joints usually exceed 50 000, although there is overlap. A negative Gram stain is reassuring but does not exclude infection, and crystals and sepsis can coexist.
  • Changes: treat as acute gout. No empirical antibiotics are needed while he is afebrile and well, but the culture must be followed up until the final report at 5 days, with a recall for orthopaedic review and IV antibiotics if it grows anything.

rows.v: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, intracellular and extracellular

rows.n: preliminary report at 48 hours, final at 5 days

handover.label: X-ray of the left hand
handover.result:
Examination: X-ray of the left hand, PA and oblique views, 08:50.

Clinical details: 36-year-old fisherman. Sudden onset of a hot, swollen, painful left ring finger DIP joint overnight. No injury recalled. ?Fracture ?foreign body ?arthropathy.

Findings:

  • Soft tissues: soft tissue swelling around the DIP joint of the ring finger. No soft tissue gas. No radio-opaque foreign body. No soft tissue calcification.
  • Bones: no fracture. Normal bone density with no periarticular osteopenia. No periosteal reaction.
  • Joints: normal alignment, no dislocation. Joint spaces preserved throughout, including the ring finger DIP. No erosions. No osteophytes. No chondrocalcinosis.

Conclusion: soft tissue swelling around the left ring finger DIP joint. No fracture, foreign body, erosive or degenerative change.
handover.model:
• Read: soft tissue swelling at the ring finger DIP. No fracture, dislocation, foreign body or gas. Joint space preserved, with no erosions, osteophytes or chondrocalcinosis.
  • Meaning: this excludes a fracture or retained foreign body (such as a fish bone or hook fragment). Early gout usually has a normal X-ray; punched-out erosions with overhanging edges appear in chronic gout. The absence of osteophytes argues against osteoarthritis, and the absence of chondrocalcinosis against pseudogout.
  • Changes: no orthopaedic intervention is needed for the bone. The film is a baseline if he goes on to have recurrent or chronic gout.

ask: You are now calling the ED consultant. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Tan, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Tan now, here in the emergency department.
Mr Tan asks you, "Is it going to keep coming back?" Please answer him, including what he should watch out for and the follow-up he will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student in ED; Mr Tan, 36, fisherman.
  • Situation: acute monoarthritis of the left ring finger DIP; aspirate confirms gout; septic arthritis not fully excluded until culture.
  • Background: sudden onset overnight, 8 to 9/10, left-handed; self-limiting big toe attack last year; lots of seafood, red wine nightly, BMI 35, smokes 15 a day; no past history or medicines; peanut anaphylaxis.
  • Assessment: obs white zone at all three sets, afebrile, pain 8 then 7/10 after initial analgesia; hot, swollen, exquisitely tender DIP, no skin break; aspirate: urate crystals, WCC 18 000, 85% neutrophils, Gram stain negative, culture pending; CRP 38, ESR 30, WCC 11.8; urate 0.40 (can be normal in a flare, above 0.36 target); renal function normal; X-ray swelling only.
  • Recommendation: NSAID now if not already given (PPI only if GI risk factors), discharge once pain controlled, GP follow-up; ED to chase cultures to final; please review and agree.

Acute gout, left ring finger DIP (second attack): sudden night-time onset, exquisite tenderness, previous big toe attack that settled in a week, seafood, red wine, BMI 35, urate crystals on aspirate.

  • Septic arthritis (must exclude): for: hot single joint, neutrophilic fluid, raised CRP. Against: afebrile, no skin break, Gram stain negative, WCC 18 000 not above 50 000; culture pending.
  • Pseudogout (CPPD): against: age 36, needle-shaped negative crystals rather than rhomboid positive, no chondrocalcinosis.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: for: DIP joint. Against: no psoriasis, nail changes or whole-finger swelling.
  • Osteoarthritis or trauma: against: acute overnight onset, no injury, normal X-ray.

1. Rest, ice, elevation, protective splint; paracetamol.
  2. NSAID (for example naproxen 500 mg orally 12-hourly, or indometacin 50 mg orally 8-hourly) until settled; a good choice for him. PPI if GI risk factors (previous ulcer or bleed, age over 65, anticoagulant, antiplatelet or corticosteroid use); he has none, so a PPI is optional for a short course; credit giving one or justifying leaving it out. Checks no renal disease, ulcer, NSAID-sensitive asthma, CVD or anticoagulants.
  3. Equally effective alternatives (eTG), or if NSAID unsuitable: low-dose colchicine (1 mg, then 0.5 mg an hour later; maximum 1.5 mg per course, not repeated within 3 days), best started early; warn about diarrhoea. Or prednisolone 30 mg orally daily for 3 to 5 days, or intra-articular steroid once infection excluded.
  4. Follow up synovial culture to the final report at 5 days and blood cultures; recall for orthopaedic review and IV antibiotics if positive or he deteriorates.
  5. Does not use allopurinol to treat the attack; leaves starting urate-lowering therapy to the GP with flare cover.
  6. Discharge once pain controlled: written plan, medical certificate, GP in 1 to 2 weeks.

• Plain words: gout: crystals of uric acid in the joint, the same as his toe last year; likely to recur without changes.
  • Lifestyle (at least three): lose weight, cut down alcohol, fewer prawns, mussels, red and organ meat, avoid sugary drinks, quit smoking (Quitline, GP).
  • Preventer: after two attacks, a daily tablet (allopurinol) is likely to be recommended; discussed at the GP review in 1 to 2 weeks and started once the flare has settled, after a repeat urate (2 to 4 weeks after the flare); taken long term to keep urate low; stop it and seek help for a rash. Credit-worthy extras, not required: start low, increase until urate below 0.36 mmol/L, flare cover when starting.
  • Red flags (straight back to ED): fever or shakes, spreading redness or red streaks up the hand or arm, pain getting worse despite treatment; ED will phone if the joint culture grows anything. Credit-worthy extras, not required: black stools, vomiting blood or severe stomach pain on the NSAID; diarrhoea on colchicine; 000 if very unwell.
  • Also in a strong answer (not marked): GP checks kidney function, BP and cholesterol; flare plan to start the anti-inflammatory at the first twinge.

ddx.dx: Acute gout of the left ring finger DIP joint (recurrent)
ddx.for: Sudden onset overnight of an exquisitely tender, red, hot joint, a self-limiting big toe attack last year, lots of seafood, nightly red wine and BMI 35, with monosodium urate crystals on aspirate.
ddx.against: His serum urate is within the reference range, which is common during a flare.

ddx.for: A hot, swollen single joint with neutrophilic synovial fluid, raised CRP and a mild neutrophilia in a man whose hands are exposed to injury at work.
ddx.against: He is afebrile and well with no skin break or penetrating injury, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial WCC is 18 000 rather than above 50 000, and urate crystals are present, though culture is pending.

ddx.for: An acute crystal-type monoarthritis with a sudden onset.
ddx.against: He is 36, the crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent rather than rhomboid and positive, and there is no chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.
He has no psoriasis, nail pitting or onycholysis, the swelling is confined to the joint rather than the whole finger (no dactylitis), and there are urate crystals on aspirate.

ddx.for: It involves a DIP joint in a manual worker with a high BMI.
ddx.against: The onset was overnight and severe at 36, with no pain on use or locking, and the X-ray shows a preserved joint space with no osteophytes.

ddx.dx: Traumatic injury or retained foreign body
ddx.for: He handles hooks, lines and fish all day.
ddx.against: He recalls no injury, there is no skin break, and the X-ray shows no fracture or foreign body.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations when asked, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Previous attacks, handedness, the peanut reaction, his family background and the risk factors come out only when asked. If the candidate orders analgesia with a dose, ice or a splint, the nurse confirms and the patient's pain eases to 7/10 by the end of Part 1. If results are requested, say they come in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all four results together, then ask the four questions in order. For the fourth, the person playing Mr Tan asks his questions from the Part 2 script. The source case gives no marks for history differentials if septic arthritis is never considered; item 7 reflects this and is Critical.

All observations sit in the white zone of the adult chart at all three times; the chart should show them unshaded. The PPI in item 31 is credited if given or if its omission is justified. HLA-B*5801 testing is not marked; a candidate who raises it because of his Chinese background may be noted favourably.

A high-performing candidate offers analgesia early, characterises the pain, and finds the previous big toe attack and the dietary, alcohol and weight risk factors. They actively screen for septic arthritis and for other arthritides, and clarify the peanut reaction. They examine the joint with look, feel and move, check for skin breaks, flexor sheath infection, spreading infection, other joints, tophi and psoriasis. In Part 2 they read the urate crystals as diagnostic but say that a pending culture means infection is not fully excluded, and that a normal urate is expected in a flare. They give an NSAID with a dose (and a PPI if GI risk) and know the alternatives. They counsel on lifestyle and a preventer tablet after two attacks, and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic joint history, does not consider septic arthritis or the previous attack, accepts the normal urate as excluding gout, uses allopurinol in the ED as the treatment for the attack, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute gout, second attack

Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystals forming in and around joints when urate stays high over time. A typical attack starts suddenly, often overnight, and reaches peak intensity within about 24 hours. The joint is red, hot, swollen and so tender that even a bedsheet hurts. Untreated attacks settle over 1 to 2 weeks. The first MTP joint (podagra) is the classic first site, as it was for Mr Tan last year. Later attacks can affect other joints, including the small joints of the hand. His risk factors are a diet high in seafood, nightly alcohol and obesity (BMI 35). Smoking does not cause gout but adds to his cardiovascular risk, which is already raised by gout and obesity.

Causes and triggers

  • Under-excretion of urate (about 90%): renal disease, hypertension, low-dose aspirin, diuretics, hypothyroidism, alcohol.
  • Overproduction: purine-rich diet, alcohol, haematological malignancy, psoriasis, chemotherapy (tumour lysis).
  • Triggers of an attack: starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy, alcohol of any type, including wine (beer carries the highest risk of developing gout), shellfish, trauma or surgery, and acute illness.

Acute monoarthritis: septic arthritis first

Every hot, swollen single joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, because an infected joint can be destroyed within days. Fever is often absent, so a normal temperature does not exclude it. A fisherman's hands are at risk of penetrating injuries from hooks, fins and bones, so ask about them and look for skin breaks. In fishers, hand infections after marine injuries can involve Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae and Vibrio species; tell the lab about the marine exposure so it can use the right culture conditions, and discuss antibiotic choice with ID if the culture grows. In the finger, also look for flexor sheath infection: a finger held flexed, swelling of the whole finger, tenderness along the sheath, and pain on passive extension. Other differentials:

  • Pseudogout (CPPD): usually older patients and larger joints such as the knee or wrist; rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: may affect DIP joints, with psoriasis, nail pitting or onycholysis, and dactylitis.
  • Osteoarthritis: DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), pain on use, and gradual onset.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness that usually spares the DIP joints. Consider RF and anti-CCP when polyarthritis is suspected, and HLA-B27 for a seronegative spondyloarthritis picture.
  • Chronic tophaceous gout: tophi on the ears, elbows, fingers or toes.
  • Trauma: fracture or a retained foreign body.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all in the white zone of the adult chart at every set, so no vital sign is in a yellow or red zone. The pain, though, is still 7/10 after initial analgesia and needs further analgesia (an NSAID now if not already given) and medical review.
  • Joint aspiration is the key test. Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light. Crystal arthritis typically gives an inflammatory fluid (WCC above 2000 ×10^6/L with more than 50% neutrophils). Septic arthritis usually gives a WCC above 50 000, but the ranges overlap. Gram stain and culture are always sent, because crystals and infection can coexist. Synovial culture gives a preliminary report at about 48 hours and a final report at about 5 days, so the loop is not closed until the final result.
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP and ESR show inflammation but do not separate gout from sepsis. Blood cultures are taken when infection is possible. Serum urate can be normal during an attack, so it is repeated 2 to 4 weeks after the flare settles. Mr Tan's 0.40 mmol/L sits inside the lab range but above the 0.36 mmol/L treatment target, and at the saturation point of urate (about 0.40 mmol/L), which supports a high urate load even during the flare. The target is set below saturation so that existing crystals dissolve. Normal renal function makes an NSAID reasonable and means allopurinol can later be started at the usual low dose. The mildly raised ALT and GGT fit alcohol or fatty liver with BMI 35.
  • Imaging: X-ray is often normal early. Chronic gout shows punched-out erosions with overhanging edges. Ultrasound may show the double contour sign (urate on the cartilage surface), and dual-energy CT can show urate deposits. Neither is needed here because crystals were seen.

Managing the acute attack (eTG Rheumatology: gout)

  • Rest, ice and elevation of the joint. Start treatment as early as possible.
  • NSAIDs, low-dose colchicine and corticosteroids are similarly effective; choose by comorbidity. For a young man with normal renal function and no ulcer history, an NSAID is a good choice.
  • NSAID (for example naproxen 500 mg orally 12-hourly, or indometacin 50 mg orally 8-hourly) until the attack settles. Add a PPI if he has GI risk factors (previous ulcer or bleed, age over 65, anticoagulant, antiplatelet or corticosteroid use); Mr Tan has none, so a PPI is optional for a short course. Check first for renal impairment, peptic ulcer, cardiovascular disease, NSAID-sensitive asthma and anticoagulants.
  • Colchicine: use the low-dose regimen (1 mg, then 0.5 mg an hour later; maximum 1.5 mg per course, and do not repeat the course within 3 days), which works as well as older high-dose regimens with far less diarrhoea. It is most effective when started early in the attack. Reduce or avoid it in renal impairment and with interacting drugs.
  • Corticosteroid: a short course of oral prednisolone (for example 30 mg orally daily for 3 to 5 days), or an intra-articular injection once infection has been excluded.
  • Do not start urate-lowering therapy as the treatment for an attack. Starting it during a flare is acceptable when anti-inflammatory cover is in place, but in the ED it is reasonable to leave this to the GP. If a patient is already taking it, do not stop it.

Preventing further attacks

  • Lifestyle: weight loss, less alcohol, fewer purine-rich foods (shellfish, red and organ meat), fewer sugar-sweetened drinks, and stopping smoking.
  • Urate-lowering therapy is recommended for recurrent attacks, tophi, erosive change, urate kidney stones or chronic kidney disease. Allopurinol is first line. Start at a low dose and increase gradually to a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, then continue long term. Febuxostat and probenecid are alternatives. Starting therapy can trigger flares, so give prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine, or a low-dose NSAID or prednisolone) for the first months. Check renal function first. Consider HLA-B*5801 testing in people of Han Chinese, Korean or Thai ancestry, who have a higher risk of severe allopurinol hypersensitivity; Mr Tan's family is Chinese, so his GP should consider this before starting allopurinol. Tell every patient to stop it and seek help if a rash develops.
  • Gout is linked with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular disease, so screen for these.

Safety netting and follow-up

Before discharge, tell the patient in plain words to come back to ED for fever, shakes, spreading redness, red streaks up the arm, pus or worsening pain, and to call 000 if very unwell. Tell him to stop the NSAID and seek help for black stools, vomiting blood or severe stomach pain, and to stop colchicine if diarrhoea develops. The ED must follow up the synovial culture until the final report at about 5 days, and the blood cultures, and phone him if anything grows. He can return to the boat when the pain settles and he can grip, usually within a week, with a medical certificate. The GP reviews him in 1 to 2 weeks to discuss the preventer tablet, repeats the urate 2 to 4 weeks after the flare, checks renal function, BP and cholesterol, starts allopurinol once the flare has settled, and agrees a flare plan (start the anti-inflammatory at the first twinge).
points: A hot, swollen single joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. A normal temperature does not exclude it, and crystals in the aspirate do not exclude coexisting infection, so always send Gram stain and culture and follow the culture to its final report (about 5 days).
Joint aspiration is diagnostic in gout: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals. Pseudogout gives rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals.
Serum urate can be normal during an acute attack. Repeat it 2 to 4 weeks after the flare settles; a value above 0.36 mmol/L is above the treatment target even if it is inside the lab range.

Treat an acute attack early. An NSAID, low-dose colchicine (1 mg, then 0.5 mg an hour later; maximum 1.5 mg per course) and a corticosteroid are similarly effective, so choose by comorbidity; add a PPI to an NSAID when there are GI risk factors. Do not use allopurinol to treat the attack itself.
After recurrent attacks, start allopurinol low and titrate to a urate below 0.36 mmol/L, with flare prophylaxis. Check renal function and consider HLA-B*5801 testing where ancestry makes it relevant.
Lifestyle matters: weight loss, less alcohol, fewer purine-rich foods (shellfish, red meat) and sugary drinks, plus stopping smoking and screening for cardiovascular risk.
